{"id": "17:11/q17", "question": "How does the verse fit its surrounding passage and other verses?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the verse either to guidance and judgment, the following cycle of time, or cross-references about haste.", "positions": [{"id": "17:11/q17/p1", "position": "After the Qurʾān's guidance, it rebukes people who turn from that gift and rashly invite the warned punishment.", "reasons": "Rāzī says people ignore the Qurʾān's laws and explanations; al-Kashf says they refuse its best path. Ālūsī contrasts the guide and guided or disobedient hearer. Ṭabāṭabāʾī links haste with neglect of guidance and the record of deeds. Islahi says Jews and Quraysh are invited to the straight path while blind rivals demand a sign of punishment. Kur'an Yolu points to 17:9."}, {"id": "17:11/q17/p2", "position": "The warning leads into night and day because fixed terms unfold with time despite impatient demands.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says haste cannot change an appointed term, while night and day show time passing. Elmalılı relates immediate gain to 17:18, and Study Quran cites 5:41, 5:62, 27:46, 6:57–58 and 29:29."}]}
{"id": "17:11/q18", "question": "How reliable are the ancillary reports used around this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether ancillary narrations have sufficient transmission and corroboration.", "positions": [{"id": "17:11/q18/p1", "position": "Reports from the Prophet, ʿAlī, Salmān and others are set aside when their chains and independent support are weak.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the reports on these verses in both Sunni and Shiʿi routes lack support from the Qurʾān, the Prophet or decisive reason, and their chains are weak."}, {"id": "17:11/q18/p2", "position": "A Muslim report describes Satan recognizing Adam's lack of restraint from his hollow formation.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī cites Anas ibn Mālik in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim as an ancillary report on human weakness."}]}
{"id": "17:11/q19", "question": "What grammatical analogies are cited for omitted endings and adjacent letters?", "turns_on": "The analogies concern omission of weak endings and spelling that distinguishes grammatical categories.", "positions": [{"id": "17:11/q19/p1", "position": "Arabic verse and prose can omit a final wāw or yāʾ when the preceding vowel indicates it.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ cites سندع الزبانية, ويدع الإنسان and three poetic examples for wāw, and ʿAntara's تكحلي وتخضب for feminine yāʾ with surviving kasra."}, {"id": "17:11/q19/p2", "position": "An alif after a plural wāw disambiguates it from other endings, whereas the singular root wāw has no such alif.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās reports al-Akhfash distinguishing plural marker from conjunction wāw; Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā says detached object from emphatic pronoun. Naḥḥās gives the specific plural versus root-wāw distinction."}]}

{"id": "17:13/q01", "question": "What does “every” cover here?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase ranges over all humans or only accountable persons.", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q01/p1", "position": "Every human individual is included in the expression.", "reasons": "Burhān and Itqān explain that kull with an indefinite complement ranges over its individuals; agreement can follow the complement's meaning. Alūsī links this restriction to the verse's ending."}]}
{"id": "17:13/q02", "question": "How is “every human” construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Accusative with an implicit verb versus nominative as a subject.", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q02/p1", "position": "Kullu insānin may be nominative as a subject.", "reasons": "Zajjāj says this is grammatically possible but knows no reader using it; Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads it so. {"id": "17:13/q03", "question": "What ancillary points are made about kull and textual argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q03/p1", "position": "Kull's syntax and agreement depend on its complement and position.", "reasons": "Burhān says omitted complements remain understood, with dispute over their tanwīn; Itqān says negation governing kull negates comprehensiveness."}, {"id": "17:13/q03/p2", "position": "Clear verses can counter an opponent's appeal to ambiguous ones.", "reasons": "Burhān describes redirecting argument toward transmitted evidence."}]}
{"id": "17:13/q04", "question": "What is the derivation and grammatical gender of insān?", "turns_on": "Basran sociability derivation versus Kufan forgetfulness derivation.", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q04/p1", "position": "Basrans derive it from sociability or humanity, on faʿlān.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī reports that they call the yāʾ in the diminutive unaysiyān extra and irregular; insān is common gender, as is faras."}, {"id": "17:13/q04/p2", "position": "Kufans derive it from forgetfulness, originally insiyān.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī reports that they cite the diminutive unaysiyān and explain the omitted yāʾ as simplification."}]}
{"id": "17:13/q05", "question": "What other source comments on the human subject?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q05/p1", "position": "A human may be defined as an animal in human form.", "reasons": "Jishumī prefers this first of two definitions; the competing definition is not preserved in the note."}]}
{"id": "17:13/q06", "question": "What does 'We bound' express?", "turns_on": "Inseparable attachment of deed or decree versus a claim about moral agency.", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q06/p1", "position": "God makes the person's deed or allotment inseparable from its owner.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr glosses ilzām from ordinary lazima. This entails full consequence for one's deeds."}, {"id": "17:13/q06/p2", "position": "The attribution to the person supports freely acquired action and responsibility.", "reasons": "Jishumī challenges determinism by asking why God would charge people for deeds He created. {"id": "17:13/q07", "question": "What is a person's attached ṭāʾir?", "turns_on": "Whether it identifies the person's deeds, decreed fortune, a written record, knowledge, or imposed responsibility.", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q07/p1", "position": "The person's good and evil deeds, which stay with their doer.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Ḥasan, Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, Farrāʾ, and many later exegetes give this gloss. Some include the deeds' consequences, happiness and misery; Qur'ān 99:5–6, 50:17–18, 82:10–14, 52:16, and 4:123 support preservation and recompense. Kur'an Yolu prefers deeds and obligations because the next clause names the record."}, {"id": "17:13/q07/p2", "position": "The person's allotted fate or share of good and evil, including felicity and misery.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda likens it to an allotted arrow/share (Persian bakht). Ibn Qutayba prefers the divinely decreed portion; Ṭabarī includes deeds and their outcomes while treating the share gloss as possible if it means these. Rāzī includes intellect, lifespan and provision; Durr cites lifespan and provision. Some link it to primordial knowledge and writing."}, {"id": "17:13/q07/p3", "position": "The person's book or written record is attached to him.", "reasons": "Damghānī includes the record of answers to Munkar and Nakīr. Al-Ḥasan describes an open ledger around the neck at resurrection; fetal and newborn reports picture a prewritten leaf there. Ālūsī allows its literal manner if reports are sound. Ibn Qutayba says the plain deed and allotted-share glosses both need clarification before preferring a decreed good-and-evil share."}, {"id": "17:13/q07/p4", "position": "The duty to obey divine law, which a person may fulfill or violate.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports this explanation; Kur'an Yolu renders it responsibility; Study Quran also mentions taklīf."}, {"id": "17:13/q07/p5", "position": "The person's knowledge of what he has done.", "reasons": "Tustarī specifies awareness of good and evil actions."}]}

{"id": "17:13/q11", "question": "Why is the bird bound specifically in the neck?", "turns_on": "Whether the image draws on collars, visible marks, obligation idioms, or a literal record.", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q11/p1", "position": "A collar, necklace, or shackle depicts an inescapable bond, honor, or shame.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says the neck bears identifying marks, adornments and shame; Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn Kathīr and others cite Arabic usage and poetry by al-Aʿshā or a dove's collar. {"id": "17:13/q13", "question": "Does naming the neck for a person affect emancipation formulas?", "turns_on": "Whether neck and throat designate the whole person differently from hand or hair.", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q13/p1", "position": "Saying a person's neck or throat is free emancipates them; saying hand or hair is free does not.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī reports Abū Ḥanīfa's legal analogy from the neck representing the whole person."}, {"id": "17:13/q13/p2", "position": "Either sort of expression emancipates the person.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī reports al-Shāfiʿī's treatment of the expressions alike."}]}
{"id": "17:13/q14", "question": "What reports or views accompany discussion of protection hung at the neck?", "turns_on": "Explanations of protective invocation range from discipline of the self to aid through spirits or divine power.", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q14/p1", "position": "An invocation may be written and hung on the neck of a child unable to recite it.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar taught the words to older children and hung a written copy on younger ones. {"id": "17:13/q16", "question": "Where is the record kept, and what happens to it from life to resurrection?", "turns_on": "Whether a recording scroll is folded and reopened, a prenatal decree hangs on the neck, or emergence means revelation of a hidden record.", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q16/p1", "position": "Two angels keep a ledger during life; it is folded at death, stays with the person in the grave, and opens at resurrection.", "reasons": "Ḥasan's account is widespread, drawing on 50:17; Abū al-Sawwār urges people to fill the open page as they choose. {"id": "17:13/q31", "question": "What ancillary rhetorical examples are cited near discussion of the verse?", "turns_on": "The examples concern poetic compression, omitted objects, or verse endings.", "positions": [{"id": "17:13/q31/p1", "position": "A pilgrimage poem exemplifies apt metaphor, economical wording and order that makes a scene immediately understood.", "reasons": "Jurjānī says its compressed completion of rites and wiping of corners indicate farewell circumambulation and departure."}, {"id": "17:13/q31/p2", "position": "Omitting understood objects can focus on actions and generalize their force.", "reasons": "Jurjānī analyses four omitted objects and examples of a mother being wearied and chambers that warm and shade; naming an object would narrow the assertion."}, {"id": "17:13/q31/p3", "position": "A clausal modifier precedes a single-word modifier here for the verse ending.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Ṣāʾigh lists this among many rhyme adjustments such as fronting governed words, pronouns and later events, or altering final letters and vowels."}]}

A Kashf al-Asrār report's king makes his self recount each evening's words, deeds, movements and stillness, which it finds hard to bear even for one day."}, {"id": "17:14/q22/p2", "position": "In choosing among worthy acts, perform the one nearer to and weightier with God first.", "reasons": "Sahl's context concerns duties, sunnas and voluntary acts; Tustarī presents this as practical self-accounting."}]}
{"id": "17:14/q23", "question": "Where does self-accounting take place?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:14/q23/p1", "position": "It may be private between servant and God or public between the person and others.", "reasons": "Sahl gives both spheres as forms of self-accounting."}]}
{"id": "17:14/q24", "question": "Why can a person be said to have authored their book?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:14/q24/p1", "position": "The person's own acts dictated its contents.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh says people should read the book because they themselves dictated it; Study Quran's reported image makes memory dictate the record while tongue, saliva and limbs form its writing implements."}]}
{"id": "17:14/q25", "question": "How does this account connect with the preceding passage?", "turns_on": "Which preceding theme supplies the transition to each person's record and judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "17:14/q25/p1", "position": "Revelation and warning have supplied proof, leaving no excuse when records are judged.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the completed account of signs and warning leads to the record; al-Ālūsī relays his proof of oneness, prophethood and resurrection. Kuranyolu likewise connects revelation, faith, reward and punishment to responsibility."}, {"id": "17:14/q25/p2", "position": "God's worldly and religious benefits call for obedience, which is then examined.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī give this as a second link."}, {"id": "17:14/q25/p3", "position": "Creation is for worship, and the sun, moon, night and day aid obedience that judgment assesses.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī cite 51:56; the latter says judgment asks whether people obeyed or rebelled."}, {"id": "17:14/q25/p4", "position": "The passage moves from God's guidance-book to the person's exhaustive deed-book.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī cites 18:49: the personal book shows whether the first book was followed."}, {"id": "17:14/q25/p5", "position": "The precise personal record makes the preceding general declaration of God's knowledge concrete.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr links encouragement and warning to 17:9–12, saying specific human deeds follow the general 'everything' for emphasis."}, {"id": "17:14/q25/p6", "position": "Human haste and desire in the surrounding rebuke explain why the enduring deed-record must be reviewed.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says people confuse benefit and harm and pursue desires though every act remains with its doer."}, {"id": "17:14/q25/p7", "position": "The larger section calls Jews and Quraysh to the straight path and contrasts acceptance with rejection.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says it rebukes demands for punishment by people blind to signs and alludes to God's treatment of nations."}]}
{"id": "17:14/q26", "question": "How does this verse illustrate the seven revealed modes in a reported classification?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:14/q26/p1", "position": "It exemplifies the mode concerning resurrection and accounting.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports a ninth explanation of the seven modes as knowledge types: creation, unity, transcendence, attributes, commands, mercy and punishment, resurrection and accounting, and prophethood; it gives this verse as the accounting example. Al-Qāḍī says all seven noncontradictory transmitted modes entered the codex except nonmutawātir material; al-Ṭabarī and most later scholars favored one, al-Shāṭibī distinguished Abū Bakr's and ʿUthmān's compilations, and al-Ṭaḥāwī viewed the modes as temporary recitation ease."}]}
{"id": "17:14/q27", "question": "What related reading and syntax issues are reported for the preceding verse?", "turns_on": "The two notes treat distinct issues in the preceding verse.", "positions": [{"id": "17:14/q27/p1", "position": "The doubled laqqā governs two objects, and its passive leaves one as subject and one as object.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī gives the transitivity and passive parse."}, {"id": "17:14/q27/p2", "position": "Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read the qāf with imāla, while the unchanged vowel is also acceptable.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī accepts both pronunciations."}]}
{"id": "17:14/q28", "question": "What ancillary rhetorical observations are included among the source notes?", "turns_on": "The notes discuss separate rhetorical examples alongside the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "17:14/q28/p1", "position": "Verb-first interrogation can deny the action's occurrence or propriety.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says such a question may challenge an impossible boast or condemn a proposal; 11:28 illustrates the latter. A figurative impossible-act question compares boast or hope to absurdity rather than asserting literal expectation."}, {"id": "17:14/q28/p2", "position": "Noun-first interrogation directs doubt to the alleged actor's identity or capacity.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī distinguishes it from action-focused questioning. In 'Would he kill me while the sword is beside me?', the sword is an impediment even though the actor could kill."}, {"id": "17:14/q28/p3", "position": "The aim of such interrogatives is to make the listener reconsider, feel shame, desist or fall silent.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī treats 'denial' as a label for this effect."}, {"id": "17:14/q28/p4", "position": "A cited Bedouin couplet and related images are praised for their figurative force.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī singles out خسأت, says dawn 'permits' sight because daylight removes night's hindrance, praises the al-Jāḥiẓ couplet and Bashshār's boil image, and finds 'toil as bridge to comfort' stronger than another bridge use, also citing Rabīʿa al-Raqqī."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q01", "question": "What does karramnā mean and convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the word denotes qualities and distinction alone or includes material wealth.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q01/p1", "position": "God conferred dignity, nobility, excellence, and manifold merits on humans.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and Majāz say the doubled form is stronger than akramnā; Jishumī says takrīm suggests repeated or abundant honor. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn derive the causative from karuma, comparing a noble garment or horse; they exclude a merely monetary sense. Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Jawzī survey karīm as noble, excellent, forgiving or beautiful; Damghānī relates it to divine favor, citing 89:15 and 17:62."}, {"id": "17:70/q01/p2", "position": "Honor includes both spiritual dignity and material wealth or blessings.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu explicitly includes material wealth alongside nobility and spiritual qualities; Bursevī describes dignity and generosity."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q02", "question": "Which of Adam's children receive this honor?", "turns_on": "Whether the dignity is common to the human kind, collective because of some members, or restricted to believers.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q02/p1", "position": "All humanity, including believers and unbelievers, receives a common worldly dignity.", "reasons": "Wasitī distinguishes universal honor from Adam's election. Ibn al-Jawzī says abundant blessings apply even to disgraced unbelievers. Ṭabrisī lists form, subjected things, and messengers. Bursevī and Abū al-Suʿūd, Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ṭabāṭabāʾī read the statement of humankind as a kind; Bursevī's inward source distinguishes common bodily and spiritual honors from prophethood, faith, and sainthood."}, {"id": "17:70/q02/p2", "position": "The group is called honored because some members possess the quality.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī and Ṭabrisī cite 'best community' at 3:110 as a collective description grounded in qualified members."}, {"id": "17:70/q02/p3", "position": "The intended children are believers.", "reasons": "Qushayrī cites 22:18: one God humiliates cannot be honored; Bursevī reports that believers' faith and deeds constitute outward honor."}]}
